## Intent
Hypothesis: an identity-ordered walk with no intermediate buffers can approach the streaming bandwidth ceiling for particle-to-grid deposition.

## Cache saturation
At q=0.01, ns/particle falls from 9.538 at N=4000 to 5.943 at N=65000 — overhead amortization dominates below N=16000, then cost stabilizes. The L1d spill (N≈963) lies below the smallest measured point, so its effect is invisible. Critically, the L2→DRAM spill at N≈61680 produces no knee: cost stays FLAT at 5.95 through N=262000 and rises only marginally to 6.203 at N=4M. Death rate raises the floor without altering the N-shape: the stable floor moves from ~5.95 ns/p (q=0.01) to ~6.4 (q=0.05) to ~8.5 (q=0.25), but every curve is high at N=4000 and flat by N=16000. The absence of any spill knee confirms the algo is not streaming-bandwidth-limited by the particle array.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved is 11.44 GB/s at N=65000, q=0.01 — 45.4% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling. At q=0.05 the peak is 10.68 GB/s (42.3%); at q=0.25 it drops to 8.11 GB/s (32.2%). The algo is overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound: it never reaches half of ceiling in any regime, and bandwidth is flat or slightly declining across N rather than rising toward ceiling at large N. Death rate is the dominant bandwidth driver — each increase in q reduces achieved bandwidth proportionally, consistent with branchy per-particle respawn logic adding overhead. The transition is by death rate, not by N.

## Assembly
The compiler did not vectorize — the histogram shows 0 vector-suffixed instructions. All floating-point work is scalar: `ldp s5, s6` loads two 4-byte floats, `fmul`, `fadd`, `fsub`, `fcvtzs` operate on scalar `s` registers. There is no `ldr q`, no NEON arithmetic, no gather. The grid scatter is byte-granular: `ldrb`/`strb` pairs (12 and 16 instances) perform read-modify-write on individual RGBA bytes with `csel` saturation to 0xff, repeated for 3 channels plus a mask byte per particle. `mul w17, w16, w21` and `lsl x1, x1, #2` compute indexed pixel offsets. This scalar byte-scatter codegen directly explains the 45% ceiling: read-modify-write byte stores cannot stream, and branch-heavy bounds checking (24 `cmp`, 20 `csel`, 6 `ccmp`, 4 `tbnz`) adds per-particle overhead that no vectorization amortizes.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo never exceeds 45.4% of the 25.22 GB/s streaming ceiling (11.44 GB/s at N=65000, q=0.01) because the compiler emits entirely scalar code with zero vector instructions and byte-granular `ldrb`/`strb` scatter stores that cannot stream. The flat N-curve with no L2-spill knee confirms the bottleneck is per-particle scatter overhead, not memory bandwidth. Death rate raises the floor from 5.95 to 8.53 ns/p without changing the shape, further indicating compute-bound rather than bandwidth-bound behavior.
